Author: @jacktattersall9457
Content: A similar differentiation can happen internationally too. Air Canada has very decent use of their two (formerly three, RIP YVR to Melbourne flight) daily flights from Vancouver to Australia (Sydney and Brisbane). A big part of this is because Air Canada can afford to time the flight better than Qantas, arriving in Vancouver in the morning but departing late at night. This allows for seamless connection to morning flights to onward Canadian destinations and the reverse for afternoon domestic flights connecting to its Australian longhaul. The flight to Sydney is even marketed as a direct one-stop because the same aircraft is used for a leg between Toronto and Vancouver. Qantas lacks this option, so lands in Vancouver in the evening, which requires passengers travelling beyond Vancouver to connect to red-eye transcontinentals on WestJet. Air Canada's flights also benefit from a seamless connection where Canadian customs takes place without needing to reclaim luggage or exit the secure area and repeat security.

I've seen this exact pattern unfold here in Morocco. Last year United launched a seasonal flight to Marrakech, the first US carrier to do so. Author: @lcloutier
Content: It seems naive to assume that only consumer market forces ("fundamentals") are driving route planning for major int'l airlines. Dealmaking is an immense part of that whole industry. This is largely the reason there are so many 3rd party airfare sellers; it's also well established that regional tourism boards are very keen to sustain routes to secondary cities inside their areas to show that they do something (including paying airlines to keep up these routes). And there's the landing fees cost cutting, as popularized by Ryanair : it's possible to undercut competitors for discount seats if you fly to a secondary airport or a 'close-enough' city gaining more margin with the lower fees including landing and other ancillary destination airport costs.

Author: @jameshumphreys2754
Content:
I love this video, but would like to add a number of pieces I think you missed for potential future video or more in depth space on each of the US legacy carriers.  

First, on general route strategy, remember that United has no choice but to be more aggressive in planning and trying to induce demand.  The reason, they are the 4th carrier by passenger volume in the US, beneath Delta (1) AA (2) and Southwest (3).  Breadth matters or they would collapse.  I think you are spot on with AA and its need for cross country traffic and Latin America traffic as a result of the Southwest hub focus.  But I think you missed the mark on Delta by a fair amount. Delta does have the smallest route network, but flies more passengers than any airline in the US.  Part is brand loyalty, part is about Delta's real defense of their Hub network and part is they get more right about getting people from where they are to where they want to go. They also have the 3rd largest fleet with AA (1) and United (2), which means that to fly more people, Delta has a higher load factor and is better at managing its fleet and demand.  In other words again, Delta gets where people want to go, better.

Part of this is about the weakness of the HUB systems that United and AA have compared to Delta.  Delta is also more profitable as a result of having the strongest hub network of the mainline carriers in the US.  Let me be specific.  United doesn't have a single hub or focus city that it dominates, except Guam.

San Fransisco - United, Southwest, Alaska
LA - United,  Delta, American, Southwest
DEN - United, Southwest, Frontier
Houston - United, Southwest
Chicago  -  United, American, Southwest
Washington - United, American, Southwest
New York - United, Delta, Jet Blue, American
Guam - United

American is not as bad but close
LA - American, Delta, United, Southwest
Phoenix - American, Southwest
Dallas - American, Southwest
Miami - American, Jet Blue, Spirit
Chicago - American, United, Southwest
Washington - American, United, Southwest
New York - American, United, Delta, Jet Blue
Charlotte - American
Philadelphia - American

Delta is King here
Atlanta - Delta
Detroit, - Delta
Minneapolis - Delta
Salt Lake City  - Delta
New York - Delta, United, Jet Blue, American
Boston - Delta, Jet Blue
Seattle - Delta, Alaska

So as you can see they dominate a larger portion of the countries population with fortress hubs with little real competition, ensuring not only loyalty but also commanding better pricing in general in its fortress cities. 

Lastly, Delta has generally better partners when it comes to where people want to fly.  Yes, United and American have a lot more Mexican cities they fly too, but Delta has a large ownership stake in Aeromexico and therefore with their US city paring gets more Americans to Mexico, through both themselves and their partner, then either United or American do.  This is also the case with other large destination places.  More American go to Europe than Asia, so having 2 major Euorpean partners keeps Delta on par with American and United with less direct costs. Delta also has ownership in LatAm for more South American connection without using its own direct resources.  The more integrated use of partner airlines is done better by Delta, than United or American on US soil, therefore moving more people from where they are are to where they want to go.

I hope this is insightful and worthy of your review.

Author: @nugnug501
Content:
The concept you're referencing is called "tacit collusion" in economics. Tacit collusion is when firms don't undercut each other's prices, which creates an artificially high price for consumers, without directly communicating with one another. 

For instance, let's say an Exxon Mobil gas station and a BP gas station are across the street from each other. One morning, the Exxon manager sees that BP's price is $2.60/gal. He decides to drop their price to $2.50 to gain more of the market share. For the next few days, all of the customers driving by go to Exxon and their short term profit goes up. But, after a few days, the BP manager realizes this and drops their own price to $2.50/gal to attract more consumers. Now, both of their prices are at $2.50/gal instead of at $2.60/gal, but the market share for each gas station is still the same as it was before, so they both just end up losing money (profits = price * quantity - costs; price goes down while quantity and costs stay constant). Therefore, knowing this, the Exxon and BP managers may decide never to undercut their competitor so that they both benefit from higher prices.

Direct collusion is illegal (like if Delta, American, and United were all on a conference call and agreed they'd all increase fares between Chicago and Boston by $100). But tacit collusion has a similar negative impact on the economy and can't really be prevented by law. This is especially true in the age of the algorithm -- each airline's uses an AI algorithm to determine prices, which certainly uses as input data the prices of their competitors on the same route, meaning each fare's price is partially determined by their competitors' prices for the same itinerary. This is basically data-driven tacit collusion. The end result is needlessly higher prices for consumers, and deadweight loss for the economy as a whole.

That being said, airlines tend to have much slimmer profit margins compared to other F500 companies, usually under 5%. So, it's hard to argue that consumers are getting ripped off when prices are barely exceeding costs, and, of course, prices have declined dramatically in the past few decades.

Author: @1MinuteMovies42
Content:
*   **Oligopoly & Convergence:** Major US airlines (United, American, Delta) operate in an oligopoly, leading them to offer very similar products (legroom, fees, reliability, etc.) to avoid mutually harmful price or product competition.
*   **Competition through Network:** With limited competitive avenues in product and price, the main arena for competition is the design of their route networks, each subtly carving out a niche.
*   **United's Strategy: Network Depth/Globality:**
    *   Focuses on serving the *highest number* of destinations with the *fewest* flights/passengers (breadth over depth).
    *   More willing to take risks on launching non-stop routes to potentially underserved markets, hoping to "induce demand" (e.g., DC-Anchorage, Christchurch, Tahiti, Cape Town).
    *   Leverages mini-hubs outside the US (like Tokyo Narita, Hong Kong) to offer unique international itineraries leveraging Guam-based aircraft or strategic timing (e.g., flights into Southeast Asia).
    *   Exploits competitive weaknesses of European joint venture partners (Lufthansa Group) by flying directly to destinations southwest of their main hubs.
    *   This strategy has positioned United well for the recent growth in long-haul international leisure travel.
*   **American's Strategy: Short-Haul Dominance & Scale:**
    *   Focuses on its "short-haul network as the foundation" and is the largest airline by *passenger count*.
    *   More conservative/risk-averse in route planning compared to United.
    *   Relies heavily on its joint venture partner (British Airways) hub in London Heathrow for international connectivity, flying a massive number of daily flights there due to limited widebody fleet.
    *   Primarily competes domestically by dominating specific regional markets, especially in the fast-growing Sun Belt (Arizona, Texas, Florida) due to geographically advantageous hubs (Dallas, Phoenix, Miami, LA) aligning with passenger flows.
    *   Extends this dominance into Latin America and the Caribbean from its southern hubs.
*   **Delta's Strategy: Premium Brand & Cost Management:**
    *   Positions itself primarily as a "premium brand" with superior service and consistently high on-time performance (though objective product differences are minimal post-COVID).
    *   Relies more on brand loyalty and cost management than its network design, which is not considered its core strategic advantage.
    *   Its network sits somewhat in the middle of United's breadth and American's domestic dominance, with some hubs being geographically less optimal than competitors'.
    *   Atlanta is the "crown jewel" hub, ideally located for capturing major North-South and East-West passenger flows and dominating connectivity in the American South.
*   **Overall Differentiation:** While major airlines appear similar on the surface, their competitive edge is primarily found in the subtle, strategic design and focus areas of their route networks (United's global reach/risk, American's Sun Belt/short-haul dominance, Delta's brand/cost efficiency).

Author: @cv990a4
Content:
Little discussion of the impact of hub size. Atlanta is a superhub - the largest in the US. This means Delta has substantially higher average aircraft size (by seats) there. So it has economies of scale - flights that, at another airport, would be flown by an RJ, at Atlanta are flown by a narrowbody. So, Delta has lower cost per passenger there. That, in turn, feeds into being able, on the margin, to offer more flights - more frequency, more destinations, etc, because cost per passenger is so low and flows are so high.

American has similar advantages at its DFW superhub, which is not quite as big as Atlanta, but certainly larger than anything else.

United lacks a superhub, which is one of the big differences between its operation and that of American and Delta. Overall, Chicago O'Hare is huge, but the operation is split between United and American, so United's Chicago hub is materially smaller than Delta at Atlanta or American at Dallas. 

Also, one reason United can fly so many transatlantic flights is they're from Newark, where it has the largest New York City metro area operation. Not only does the NYC area have huge intrinsic demand, but United can connect over Newark.

Delta can't do that, not to the same extent, because while it is large at JFK airport in New York City, it is slot-constrained. If it was able to offer the same number of flights out of JFK as United was out of Newark, Delta would likely offer some of those "near-international" locations as well. But it can't. So it does the best it can with what it has.

Further, the potential of Dulles airport in DC and JFK in NYC is damaged by the so-called "perimeter rules" that split out shorter haul traffic to Washington Reagan National and Laguardia airports respectively. Without that perimeter rule, the traffic flows would be better balanced between long-haul/short haul at Dulles and JFK, which would make those better hubs (you need a mix of short and long-haul traffic). 

This video wasn't a bad intro to Big Airline network, but it didn't dig as deep as maybe it could have.

Author: @21jc21
Content: Another thing is that Delta is far more invested in its Joint Ventures compared to United and American, to the point where DL partially owns other airlines (which I don't think UA and AA do). They own 49% of Virgin Atlantic (can't go any higher due to UK laws), 20% of LATAM, 20% of AeroMexico, and a small portion of Air France/KLM. They also have their JV with Korean Airlines as well, and I think they did own part of Virgin Australia before backing out due to COVID. They essentially outsource their international network to them, or focus on flights to Paris, Amsterdam, Mexico City, Lima, and Seoul, and let their partners do the rest of the work. It's similar to what AA does with British Airways in London, but to a much larger scale, and to the point where it's even been a point of contention with their pilot's union.
